source.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
source.authors: Srikanth Malla; Chi-Ho Choi; J. Choi

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports experiments on activation-steering interference and whether behavior-direction geometry predicts it, but it does not test feature superposition, capacity pressure, SAE features, or whether model features are one-dimensional. Its direction-versus-cone results concern steering interference rather than the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The text describes and tests a related geometric account of steering interference, not superposition or the representation claims in the listed versions. The rows below record relevant findings about behavior directions and steering interference under versions ["none"]. The paper also reports decodability and calibration details, but these do not directly test a listed version.
record.test_reason: The study measures activation-steering interference among 24 behavior directions in instruction-tuned LLMs, judged from generated text. It does not study superposition, feature sparsity versus dimension, polysemantic neurons, SAEs, or whether features are one-dimensional. It never mentions superposition and does not cite the original source. The 3-dim concept cone comparison asks only whether a richer direction estimate predicts interference better. It does not ask whether features are multi-dimensional, so it does not test V6. Linear decodability of behaviors is not evidence about features spread across neurons or recoverable by a dictionary, so it does not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that what a steer moves is set by the model's default set (e.g., refusal, sycophancy, poeticism), not by the geometry of the steered direction. Random pushes reproduce the ranking, and geometry predicts held-out interference poorly. The default pull weakens in each family's largest model. They make no claim about superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures activation-steering effects and tests whether behavior-direction geometry predicts text-judged interference; it does not reproduce the original toy-model superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The random-push/default-susceptibility correlation weakens in each family’s largest tested model; the particular default behaviors vary by model and alignment style. The results also depend on whether effects are read from generated text rather than activation probes.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, steering interference is largely one-way (antisymmetric norm fraction 0.68). A norm-matched random direction reproduces the susceptibility ranking of real steers (Spearman 0.90). Leave-one-behavior-out geometry predicts held-out interference weakly (best Spearman 0.41, R2 below 0.10). These patterns replicate across ten models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-behavior steering side effects are driven by model-specific default susceptibilities rather than by the overlap of the steered behavior directions.

fits_no_version.finding: All 24 behaviors are linearly decodable (held-out AUROC 1.00), yet only 20 are steerable from text. Modelling a behavior as a 3-dim concept cone instead of a single direction does not improve interference prediction (cone overlap Spearman -0.21, R2 -0.030).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linear decodability of a behavior direction does not imply causal steerability. Multi-dimensional behavior subspaces do not explain steering interference better than single directions.

record.problems: The detailed map is built on one model, though the authors report replication on nine further instruction-tuned models. All models judge their own generations in the main study; a fixed-judge ablation is reported for three models. The study uses the same 24 behaviors across models. The authors note that most pairwise interference is explained neither by geometry nor by the one-way ranking, and that the reason the default pull weakens at the largest scale is unexplained.

untested.parts: All: toy-model storage of sparse features as nearly orthogonal overlapping directions, the sparsity transition, and the geometry.
All: capacity competition as the cause of polysemantic neurons.
All: features spread across neurons, or sparse features recovered by an SAE, in LLMs. Behavior directions are only shown to be linearly decodable.
All: completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.
All: whether superposed features are 1-D. The cone-vs-direction comparison concerns interference prediction only.

record.verdict_notes: All rows are correctly linked to ['none'], and their values match the text (r1 +3.4, r2 +0.0, r3 0.68, r4 0.90, r5 0.41, r6 0.092, r7 -0.03). The relation 'discusses' is generous: the paper neither discusses nor cites superposition and works within a linear-direction framing. No verdicts are given because no version is tested.

versions.untested_parts: Whether sparse features exceeding network dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions; sparsity-dependent transitions and regular geometry.
Whether feature competition for capacity causes polysemantic neurons or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises through mechanisms other than capacity pressure.
Whether LLM features spread across neurons or sparse features can be recovered with a dictionary or SAE.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representation.
Whether the features involved in superposition are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional features.
